events.description: Day 4 at 10:22: Patient activated monitor reporting palpitations and lightheadedness. Recording shows abrupt onset of regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 218 bpm lasting 38 seconds, terminating spontaneously with abrupt return to sinus rhythm. RP interval short; P waves visible as retrograde deflections immediately following QRS in the ST segment (pseudo-S waves in leads II, III, aVF). Patient diary: 'heart racing very fast, nearly fainted.'

Day 9 at 14:48: Monitor auto-detected rapid heart rate while patient was seated at rest. Recording shows abrupt onset of regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 224 bpm lasting 12 seconds, terminating spontaneously. Same morphology as Day-4 event. Patient diary entry at 14:51: 'sudden racing, went dizzy, almost blacked out again. Sat down quickly.'
All tachycardia episodes: regular rhythm, narrow QRS complex (87 ms), rate 218-224 bpm, abrupt onset and termination, no visible distinct P waves before QRS during tachycardia
Baseline rhythm between events: normal sinus rhythm, rate 58-88 bpm, normal PR interval, no pre-excitation pattern, no delta waves
No atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter detected during the monitoring period
No sustained ventricular tachycardia. Isolated PVCs: 14 total over 14 days, no couplets.
No significant pauses (maximum RR interval 1.12 seconds during sinus rhythm)

findings: Two episodes of paroxysmal regular narrow-complex tachycardia at rates 218-224 bpm, with abrupt onset and termination, captured during patient-reported palpitations
Retrograde P-wave morphology (pseudo-S waves in inferior leads, pseudo-R' in V1) during tachycardia consistent with short RP tachycardia
Both episodes temporally correlated with diary-documented palpitations and near-syncope or presyncope
Baseline sinus rhythm between events: normal, no pre-excitation
No atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, or ventricular tachycardia detected
Isolated PVCs: 14 total over 14 days (0.003% burden), no couplets
output.impression: 14-day event monitor demonstrates two episodes of paroxysmal regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 218-224 bpm with abrupt onset and termination, retrograde P-wave morphology (short RP pattern), and temporal symptom correlation with patient-documented palpitations and near-syncope. Baseline rhythm is normal sinus rhythm without pre-excitation. No atrial fibrillation, flutter, or ventricular tachycardia captured.
output.rhythm_summary: Predominantly normal sinus rhythm; two episodes of paroxysmal regular narrow-complex tachycardia at approximately 218-224 bpm captured with symptom correlation

results.authors: Page RL, Joglar JA, Caldwell MA, et al.
results.summary: Catheter ablation of the slow AV-nodal pathway is recommended (Class I) for symptomatic AVNRT when arrhythmia causes significant symptoms or syncope. Acute termination with vagal maneuvers (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) or intravenous adenosine is the first-line approach. Catheter ablation has a success rate exceeding 95% with a low recurrence rate.
results.title: 2015 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the Management of Adult Patients With Supraventricular Tachycardia

results.summary: AVNRT accounts for approximately 60% of regular narrow-complex SVT and is the most common form of paroxysmal SVT. It is more prevalent in women and in the fifth to sixth decade. Rates during tachycardia typically range 150-250 bpm; rates above 200 bpm can cause hemodynamic compromise and syncope, particularly in the absence of structural heart disease where abrupt high ventricular rates markedly reduce cardiac output.
results.title: Epidemiology and Natural History of Supraventricular Tachycardias

results.authors: Brembilla-Perrot B, Moulin-Zinsch A, Sellal JM, et al.
results.summary: Among patients presenting with syncope and subsequently documented SVT, rates above 200 bpm and absence of structural heart disease were associated with syncopal episodes due to transient cerebral hypoperfusion. Rhythm documentation via event monitoring or electrophysiology study was required in the majority of cases to confirm the diagnosis, as resting ECG was normal in most.
results.title: Syncope Due to Supraventricular Tachycardia: Incidence, Clinical Features, and Outcome

alternatives: Vagal maneuvers (Valsalva, carotid sinus massage) as first-line for acute termination
Intravenous adenosine for acute termination if vagal maneuvers fail
Catheter ablation for definitive long-term management per electrophysiology evaluation
contraindications: AV-nodal blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers) are contraindicated if a pre-excitation syndrome (WPW) is present or cannot be excluded, as they may preferentially block the AV node and facilitate rapid accessory-pathway conduction during atrial fibrillation.
interactions: Verapamil / Diltiazem / Beta-blockers: slow AV-nodal conduction and are used for rate control in regular SVT without pre-excitation; see contraindications section for pre-excitation caveat.
Adenosine IV: no clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction with lorazepam or levothyroxine at standard doses; caution in reactive airway disease.
Lorazepam + beta-blockers: additive sedation possible at high doses; clinical monitoring appropriate.
output.proposed: AV-nodal agents for rate control or rhythm management in SVT (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, adenosine IV); review interaction with lorazepam and levothyroxine
warnings: Confirm absence of ventricular pre-excitation (delta waves, short PR) on resting ECG and monitor strip before initiating AV-nodal blocking therapy.
Lorazepam (benzodiazepine): not an antiarrhythmic; inappropriate as treatment for arrhythmia-mediated syncope.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not dismiss recurrent syncopal episodes with preceding rapid palpitations as panic attacks or vasovagal syncope without rhythm documentation

Do not administer AV-nodal blocking agents (verapamil, diltiazem, beta-blockers, digoxin) if ventricular pre-excitation (WPW pattern) cannot be excluded on resting ECG and ambulatory monitoring, as these agents can precipitate ventricular fibrillation via accessory-pathway conduction
Do not use lorazepam as treatment for arrhythmia-mediated palpitations or syncope
Do not discharge home without a cardiac monitoring plan when rhythm has not yet been documented
required_recommendations: Obtain 12-lead ECG immediately to evaluate for pre-excitation (WPW) or other structural conduction disease
Arrange prolonged cardiac event monitoring to capture the tachyarrhythmia during symptoms and establish symptom-rhythm correlation
Teach vagal maneuvers (supine Valsalva, modified Valsalva) for patient self-use to terminate future AVNRT episodes
Administer intravenous adenosine for acute termination if patient presents in SVT and vagal maneuvers fail
Refer to cardiology / electrophysiology for catheter ablation of the slow AV-nodal pathway as definitive management
Counsel patient on driving restriction until the arrhythmia is definitively treated

accepted: Cardiac syncope due to paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia (AVNRT)

differential.key_features: Known anxiety disorder; prior physician attributed episodes to panic attack — monitoring capturing rapid regular tachycardia at 218-224 bpm during symptoms refutes this.
Syncope with palpitations requires VT exclusion; narrow QRS complex and structurally normal heart make VT unlikely.

differential.diagnosis: Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response
differential.key_features: Can cause rapid rates with syncope; irregular rhythm and absence of consistent narrow-QRS morphology on monitoring distinguish from the captured regular tachycardia.
No positional trigger, no warm environment precipitant, no typical prodrome of nausea/pallor before palpitations, tilt-table negative.
Presents with similar narrow-complex tachycardia; resting ECG and inter-episode monitoring show no delta waves or pre-excitation, making WPW-mediated AVRT less likely than AVNRT.

key_clinical_evidence: A normal resting ECG does not exclude paroxysmal SVT — the diagnosis requires rhythm capture during symptoms, which is the load-bearing role of event monitoring in this case

AVNRT at rates above 200 bpm can cause syncope from transient cerebral hypoperfusion even in the absence of structural heart disease; the mechanism is tachyarrhythmic (rapid rate), not bradycardic or structural

The anxiety disorder and prior attribution of episodes to panic attacks is the principal red herring — both panic attacks and AVNRT cause sudden palpitations, but AVNRT produces a regular, very rapid (>200 bpm), abruptly terminating rhythm captured on the monitor, which is not consistent with sinus tachycardia of anxiety
Pre-excitation must be actively excluded before AV-nodal blocking therapy; if WPW is present, these drugs are dangerous
Retrograde P-wave morphology during tachycardia (pseudo-S waves in inferior leads, pseudo-R' in V1) is a typical AVNRT finding that distinguishes it from sinus tachycardia and atrial flutter

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Panic attacks cause sinus tachycardia, not a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 218-224 bpm with abrupt onset and termination; the palpitations described by the patient precede and trigger the syncope rather than following anxiety, and the event monitor captures the true arrhythmia

red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor the diagnostic approach to an anxiety/vasovagal framework and deter cardiac rhythm work-up

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Helen Nakamura is a 52-year-old woman with a history of generalized anxiety disorder, hypothyroidism, and migraine who presents to the emergency department after a second episode of sudden loss of consciousness. Today's episode occurred approximately 90 minutes ago while she was grocery shopping. She reports that before losing consciousness she suddenly became aware of a rapid, regular fluttering sensation in her chest lasting approximately 5-10 seconds, followed almost immediately by lightheadedness and then complete loss of consciousness. A store employee witnessed the event and reported that she collapsed without warning, was unresponsive for approximately 20 to 30 seconds, then regained consciousness spontaneously and was immediately lucid and conversational. No convulsive movements were observed. She was pale and diaphoretic when she recovered. There was no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence, and no post-ictal confusion. She was seated by the time paramedics arrived approximately 6 minutes later. Paramedics documented a regular pulse at 78 beats per minute with blood pressure 116/72 mmHg and room air oxygen saturation of 99 percent. Her first episode occurred approximately 6 weeks ago while sitting at her desk grading papers. She recalls a similar sensation of sudden rapid palpitations followed immediately by loss of consciousness. She was evaluated the following morning by her primary care physician who, given her known anxiety disorder, attributed the episode to a panic attack complicated by vasovagal syncope. No cardiac testing was performed at that time and she was reassured. She continued to experience intermittent episodes of brief palpitations over the subsequent weeks, each lasting several seconds and resolving spontaneously, without loss of consciousness. She reports these palpitations are distinctly different from her usual anxiety — they come without any preceding worry or situational trigger, are sudden in onset, feel very rapid and regular, and stop abruptly. She has never experienced palpitations of this character before the first syncopal event. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, exertional dyspnea, leg swelling, or near-syncope with exertion. She denies any prior seizure history, head trauma, or family history of epilepsy or sudden cardiac death. She denies any new medications, herbal supplements, or recreational substance use.
